planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or containerized vines in early spring against a sturdy trellis or arbor in full sun.

directions: A USDA cross of Flame Tokay and Ribier released in 1939, Cardinal is prized for very early ripening large, round, deep-red berries in loose, well-filled clusters with a mild, sweet flavor. Train vines onto a permanent cordon system and prune hard each dormant season, since fruit forms on one-year-old canes. It sets heavy crops and colors up reliably in hot-summer regions but tends toward loose, uneven clusters and thin skin that bruises easily, so it is best suited to home gardens rather than long-distance shipping. Like most vinifera grapes it needs a long, warm growing season and struggles with fungal disease in humid climates.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or containerized vines in early spring in full sun against a trellis or arbor with room for vigorous growth.

directions: Released by the USDA in 1973, Flame Seedless is the most widely planted red seedless grape in the United States, valued for crisp, round, bright-red berries with a sweet, mildly fruity flavor on medium, well-filled clusters that ripen mid-season. Vines are vigorous and productive, and thinning clusters and berries early in the season improves size and air circulation. It performs best with a long, hot growing season and reliably colors well even in warm-night climates where many red grapes struggle to develop color. Prune to a permanent cordon system in dormancy and renew fruiting spurs each winter.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or containerized vines in early spring in full sun on a sturdy trellis, allowing ample room for a vigorous, spreading canopy.

directions: Released by UC Davis in 1980, Red Globe produces very large, round, rose-red berries in big, heavy clusters with a mild, sweet flavor and firm, crisp flesh that stores exceptionally well. It is a late-season variety, ripening well after most other table grapes, which makes it valuable for extending the harvest into fall. Vines are vigorous and need generous spacing and a strong support system to carry the weight of its oversized clusters, plus cluster thinning to prevent overcropping. It has seeds, distinguishing it from most modern supermarket table grapes, but its size and long storage life have kept it a mainstay variety for decades.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or containerized vines in early spring in full sun against a trellis or arbor.

directions: A USDA release from 1968, Ruby Seedless bears medium, oval, reddish-purple berries with a sweet, slightly tart flavor on large, well-filled clusters that ripen mid-to-late season. The berries can be slow to color fully, developing deeper red tones as they hang longer on the vine in warm weather. Vines are vigorous and productive, so annual dormant pruning to a permanent cordon and early-season cluster thinning help keep berry size and quality consistent. It thrives with a long, hot, dry growing season and is prone to fungal problems in humid climates.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or containerized vines in early spring in full sun on a sturdy trellis, giving room for a large, vigorous canopy.

directions: Bred by USDA researcher David Ramming and released in 1996, Autumn Royal produces very large, elongated, jet-black seedless berries with a mild, sweet flavor on large clusters that ripen quite late in the season. It extends the black seedless grape harvest well into fall, after most other black varieties have finished. Vines are vigorous and heavy-bearing, benefiting from cluster thinning and a strong permanent cordon system to support the oversized bunches. A long, warm growing season is needed to fully ripen this late-hanging variety.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or containerized vines in early spring in full sun against a trellis or arbor.

directions: Another David Ramming USDA release, introduced in 2006, Scarlet Royal produces large, firm, bright-red seedless berries with a sweet, crisp bite on very large clusters that ripen late in the season. It reliably develops strong red color even under warm-night conditions that leave some other late red grapes pale, making it a dependable choice for extending the red seedless harvest into fall. Vines are vigorous and productive, so cluster thinning and a sturdy permanent cordon system help manage the heavy crop load. It needs a long, hot growing season to size and color properly.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or containerized vines in early spring in full sun against a trellis or arbor.

directions: Marketed commercially as Superior Seedless, Sugraone is an early-ripening white seedless grape bearing large, oblong, pale green-yellow berries with a crisp texture and mild, sweet flavor on large, loose clusters. Its early maturity makes it one of the first seedless table grapes ready for harvest each season, well ahead of Thompson Seedless. Vines are vigorous, so berry and cluster thinning early in the season improves size and reduces the tight, compact clustering the variety is prone to. Gibberellic acid treatments are commonly used commercially to loosen clusters and enlarge berries, though home growers can rely on hand thinning instead.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or containerized vines in early spring in full sun against a trellis or arbor.

directions: Released by UC Davis in 1946, Perlette is one of the earliest-ripening seedless table grapes, producing small to medium, round, pale green berries with a crisp, neutral-sweet flavor on compact clusters. Its very early harvest window makes it popular with home gardeners wanting fresh grapes before most other varieties are ready. Vines are moderately vigorous and clusters tend to be tightly packed, so thinning berries when they are pea-sized helps prevent splitting and rot in humid weather. It has good cold tolerance for a vinifera type but still needs a warm, sunny site to ripen well.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or containerized vines in early spring in full sun on a sturdy trellis or arbor.

directions: A historic California table grape grown commercially since the early 1900s, Emperor produces large, round to oval, pale pinkish-red berries with a mild, sweet flavor and notably firm flesh that keeps in cold storage longer than most table grapes. It ripens very late in the season and was long the standard variety for holiday-season fresh grapes before newer red seedless types largely replaced it commercially. Vines are vigorous and long-lived, so an established permanent cordon system and annual dormant pruning keep fruiting wood renewed. It needs a long, warm season to fully ripen its late-hanging clusters.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

subcategory: seedless black table and raisin grape

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root or containerized vines in early spring in full sun against a trellis or arbor.

directions: Introduced to the United States from Central Asia in the early 20th century, Black Monukka bears small to medium, elongated, reddish-black seedless berries with a distinctly sweet, honeyed flavor on medium, loose clusters that ripen mid-season. It is one of the oldest seedless grape varieties grown in American home gardens and is well suited to both fresh eating and drying into raisins. Vines are vigorous and productive, tolerating a wider range of climates than many other vinifera table grapes, though annual dormant pruning to a permanent cordon system keeps fruiting wood renewed and clusters well formed. It benefits from a long, warm season but is somewhat more forgiving of cooler summers than late-ripening varieties.
sources: University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; the crimped foliage color and texture are best in full sun, and a light shearing after the first bloom flush keeps the mound tidy.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and shear lightly after bloom to maintain a dense, rounded shape. Crispa is a distinctive dwarf Japanese spirea grown for its deeply cut, twisted, and crimped leaf margins, which give the foliage a coarse, ruffled texture unlike the smooth leaves of most spirea cultivars, emerging reddish before settling to blue-green through summer with orange-bronze fall color. Small flat clusters of pale pink flowers appear in early summer but are secondary to the foliage interest. Its compact, low-mounding habit suits rock gardens, small-space borders, and mixed foundation plantings where an unusual texture is wanted.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; its very low, fine-textured mound needs little pruning beyond an occasional light shearing to keep it dense.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun. Daphne spirea is one of the smallest and finest-textured of the Japanese spirea selections, forming a dense, flat-topped mound of tiny, narrow blue-green leaves that stays well under a foot and a half tall, far more diminutive than the popular gold-leaved dwarf cultivars. Small, flat clusters of soft pink flowers cover the mound in early summer. Its extremely low, tidy habit makes it useful as an edging plant, in rock gardens, or massed as a low informal groundcover where taller spirea cultivars would overwhelm the space.

common_name: Double Play Blue Kazoo Spirea (Reblooming Blue-Green Foliage Compact Spirea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; deadheading the first flush of flowers encourages the summer rebloom characteristic of the Double Play series.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, and shear off the first flush of spent flower clusters to promote continued summer bloom. Double Play Blue Kazoo is a reblooming member of Proven Winners' Double Play spirea series, distinguished from its series-mates by cool blue-green summer foliage rather than gold or bicolor leaves, topped by rounded clusters of pink flowers that repeat through the season on a low, tidy mound. It is heat- and drought-tolerant once established and needs little care beyond an occasional post-bloom shearing to keep the habit dense.

common_name: Double Play Artisan Spirea (Reblooming Variegated Compact Spirea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; variegation is most pronounced in full sun, and shearing off the first flower flush encourages summer rebloom.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun, deadheading the first bloom flush to encourage the series' characteristic summer rebloom. Double Play Artisan stands out among the Proven Winners Double Play spirea introductions for its creamy white-and-green variegated foliage, which takes on pink tints in cool weather, contrasting with rounded clusters of pink summer flowers on a compact, low mound. Like other members of the series it is tough and low-maintenance, tolerating heat and drought once established, and needs only an occasional light shearing after bloom to stay dense and tidy.
